Not the best or worst lecturer, but she only tells you what you need to know for exams. Any lapses in understanding from the lecture can be easily fixed by going to discussion with the TA, reading the textbook, or by watching youtube videos. One bonus to taking chem271 with her is that there's a huge emphasis on problem solving compared to conceptual understanding, which means you only need to know how to do the calculations to do good on exams. Peers in the other section (Kahn) were actually tested on conceptual understanding, which made me thankful that I took it with her instead. Before every exam she would post a practice exam with answers, and these practice exams were 90% similar to the real exams. If you can do every question in the practice exams & understand each step, you will get an A on the real exam. 4 stars instead of 5 stars because of the ALEKS hw

Her lectures are informative and thorough. They cover a lot of material and she is good at explaining concepts. However, the lab experiments/reports require an ungodly amount of time to complete. Be prepared to pull all-nighters completing them throughout the semester. Also, the exams are very difficult. She plays with words and makes the questions very tricky, which is annoying, especially since the exams are timed and you barely have enough to rush through it.

Idk what these reviews are on about. Yoon is a good professor who gives tons of information during the lectures, makes jokes, asks questions, etc. His exams and quizzes ARE hard I agree, but he's a pretty flexible grader and he definitely prepares people for both the quizzes and the exams by providing study guides for the students and telling us what will be on the exam. If you don't get a C in this class (and I am sure many want at least a B-), it's your fault for not putting in effort and time to studying for a STEM class. It's only going to get harder from here on, and I feel Yoon has prepared us adequately. The projects take up more of your final grade anyway, and he's given tons of time to write 100 lines of code. One project had a MONTH to do it, and it was based on code we already had in a previous project!

Her lectures aren't perfect like others have mentioned, but her slides and code examples are really good for learning the content. She has weekly projects, which if you're interested in computer science are somewhat enjoyable and also teach the content quite well (if you do well on the projects, you can do well on quizzes). I would recommend her and I think she deserves higher than her current reviews suggest.

So much extra credit. Discussions are useless. Lectures are engaging. You can easily excel in the class even without touching the textbook. If you go to (or watch recordings of) all the lectures and complete all labs and homework on your own time honestly (not just copying or clicking through) it's a surprisingly easy A.
An incredible lecturer, the best I have ever had. He did get a bit too much when it came to the homeworks and the exams were a bit too much, however, he is still an incredible lecturer!!

Fardina is a very nice professor and her class is pretty chill. Her lectures are kinda mid I won't lie, but she does record them and her slides are very thorough. Homework was pretty reasonable. Whenever it included stuff not covered in class, she added links to relevant documentation. Exams were also very reasonable. She provided study guides for all exams (2 midterms and a final), and you were allowed to bring a cheatsheet for the final. The final project (which spanned the semester) was also pretty chill if you picked a good group and good dataset. The only thing that bothered me was that answer keys were always gatekept. If you wanted to see what you got wrong on a homework or exam, you had to go to office hours.
He's a great professor. He's really lenient with extensions which is something I myself have appreciated with; he is reasonable with course requirements. Definitely take.

Justin is an amazing lecturer: his explanations in-class are clear, color-coded well-written, easy to process notes, well-timed, engaging lectures. Humorous. Fair exams. Fair homeworks that are very good practice for the exams. (Class is self-contained, no need to learn anything outside the class). Very approachable and helpful with questions. I asked him about a personal project and he worked through the algorithm with me. Personally, though, I thought he made the class TOO easy. It was supposed to be a class that teaches algorithmic thinking, but we kind of were just tracing pseudocode. I trust he knows what he's doing, and I'm taking 451 anyway, but it would have been nice to learn/be tested on more. We do barely any proofs and time complexity is reduced to memorization. That being said, he provides rigorous proofs in the notes that he posts. He posts class notes and LatEx notes. He has practice exams which are very helpful, and weekly MCQ's, which also help you study. Weekly MCQ's are easy points, open note, online.

I have a love-hate relationship with this course. I have come to the conclusion, after much flip-flopping, that although Marsh has a bit of a strange protocol for running a course, he is my favorite CS instructor. At first it is a little tricky to get into his headspace, but once I had my head around the groove of the course I found it very enjoyable. I thought that the projects were fun, and that Marsh really wants his students to succeed in the course. He is always responsive and willing to help out and give feedback. Marsh himself is your most valuable resource in this course, I think. I highly recommend 414 in particular, but I would recommend Marsh as an instructor for any other course as well. I would absolutely take a class with him again.

Based on past reviews, I was extremely weary to take Marsh for this class, but after going through it I’m glad I did. He has improved a ton and takes constructive criticism in stride to actually improve the class (the only cs prof I’ve seen do this). Many complain his test scripts are still broken, but these were due to tests that are more in depth than other courses, which I believe is a great thing. You can also tell he loves the subject. His lectures can be a little tough to follow at times as his examples aren’t always the clearest, but he is willing to reexplain anything that may have been ambiguous. Overall, the most useful class I’ve taken at UMD and no regrets on Marsh.

Narayanaswamy should not be employed here. He is a very poor lecturer. He started off with handwritten notes that were extremely hard to follow and not even always fully correct. Eventually he just gave up and started presenting seemingly random slides he found on the internet. It was never easy to follow him, and he would start rambling off about unnecessary topics. He is a very poor communicator. Nobody knew what the structure of the course was going to look like till about 3 weeks in, AFTER the add/drop deadline. He gave very vague comments about how the homeworks/exams/projects would be set up and never made it clear what the grading guidelines were. For some godforsaken reason, he made most homeworks due at 12:30am, rather than 11:59pm, or any other conceivable time of day. This would cause a lot of confusion as an assignment due Nov 30 actually had to be done by the night of Nov 29. Now you think you would get used to this, except he often changed the deadlines for assignments. I was unable to submit one homework because for no real reason he decided that one will be due at 11:59. His project deadlines were even worse. They never released on time and the due date would keep getting pushed back because the description left us with too many questions about the project details. We were supposed to have 5 project but he was so late on them that we only had 4. And the projects weren't even relevant to the content we were covering, instead being about some stupid fictional world with lore and all sorts of unnecessary details. The one midterm we had (which he changed the weightage of without telling us by the way) had an average of 55%, as he gave no real study guide, or even general advice on what it would cover, how to best prepare, etc. The TAs are entirely useless and may as well not exist. They don't hold office hours and are of extremely little help. I've even seen them giving objectively wrong answers about programming projects on Piazza. Narayanaswamy himself gave up in person office hours and only holds them via Zoom, which you have to schedule via email. He is of very little help too, as once my friend went for help with some test cases for a programming project, and Narayanaswamy told him to literally "comment out blocks of his code to figure out what test cases were testing" because the instructors had improperly named the tests. Overall, this has been an extremely negative experience. I don't even think this a case where a professor can learn from a rocky first semester and improve, he is just an objectively bad teacher.

Fair professor. Lectures are kinda dry so I stopped attending lectures after first week of school since I figured out his lectures is much better in 1.5x so I basically watched his recording to learn. Slides were actually helpful and his explanations are also helping understand the course content. Project are from Berkely and majority of the contents are from Berkely. Good thing with that is you can find many resources (and he did gave some resources) so you can learn after class. Bad thing is that it is kinda boring. Exams are fair and similar to our HW. I did learn many stuffs from the course. Also the grading is fair to me. I find out the TA is tending to give more lenient grades due to the nature of some problems of the HW. Honestly he is pretty solid 3 star professor to me. Just give him 4 star because I think he desevers a little better than 2.33 stars.
Ramani is a friendly teacher, but I don't think he taught 422 that well. Lectures were sort of boring, and he doesn't really explain concepts in an intuitive, understandable way.

Enjoyed this class with Dr Abadi. You will learn a fair amount about SQL and using DBMS properly, but even more about the in depth technical details of designing databases. The first half of the class is straightforward and fun, learning about writing SQL queries and E/R models. Midterm was pretty easy if you paid attention. The material gets very very difficult towards the end of the semester. Reading quizzes get hard as the semester goes on. The projects become very time consuming and somewhat confusing as well. As always, if you start early, they are doable. Final was egregiously hard, but Dr Abadi informed us that there was a mistake made regarding the difficulty level. A quite substantial curve was provided on the final exam. Overall, would recommend, but be ready for a moderately heavy workload at times.

Not a huge fan of the lecturing style at all and I attended almost every class. Lectures are dull. Prof just reads off the slides and doesn't seem prepared for questions. He is a lot better at answering questions on Piazza than answering them during lecture. There's a lot of conceptual material but often he refers to variables/equations/concepts as "this" or "that" while lecturing—delivery could be clearer. Grading is slow. BUT, I honestly think you could get by decently in this class without attending any lectures at all. Slides are detailed and always posted to Canvas. Grades are all based on a few homework assignments and projects with very clear grading criteria and instructions. Grading is lenient with a lot of opportunities for extra credit.

Great professor who really knows the material and does a great job of teaching it to students. Very fair on exams and projects, and really treats his students with courtesy and respect. One of the best professors in the University, and a leader in the field of HCI.

The course materials are good and the assignments are very fair. However, I never knew what my grade was in the class since the homework assignments took forever to grade. Idk if it's the fault of the TAs or Katz, but it's an anxiety-inducing issue that Katz cares very little about.

(spring 2020, ~ second half online due to COVID-19, expecting A/A+ but also P since I will P/F all my classes) I was going to rate 4/5, but Dr. Manning handled the shift to the online format really well, so 5/5. The first midterm (in-class) was made really easy (mathematically) since a lot of CS majors don't have the sufficient proof-writing experience. Similarly some lectures could be really boring due to the need to explain some math concepts that some CS majors aren't familiar with (e.g. basic linear algebra). Note that on PlanetTerp (as of writing this) MATH456 has an average GPA of 2.93 while CMSC456 has an average GPA of 2.37 even though they are the same class (only math majors / cs+math double majors can register for the class as MATH456). After the class was shifted online due to COVID-19, Dr. Manning provided recorded videos (much better than forcing students to virtually attend at fixed times) and the second midterm was a ~week-long mix of theoretical questions and programming (implementing some of the algorithms described in the lectures).

Amazing teacher and will definitely help you learn Python better. I personally learned nothing from INST126 and Aric made it so I learned Python. He has a lot of TA's who are extremly helpful so office hours aren't loaded. There is a bit of work so start things early. He has 4 exams but they are only 25% of your grade. Overall would definitely recommend.

A more recent review* Professor Wilson is really easygoing and friendly teacher. He explains things thoroughly, uses a lot of examples, answers any questions. He's also fairly available and answers emails pretty quick. In terms of coursework, midterms are not too challenging; As long as you keep up with HW, worksheets, yada yada, you will most likely do well in the class. All in all, definitely recommend taking Matthew for math.

One of the worst math professors you could take. Should have at least a 2 or lower. An insane percentage of the class drops his classes, leaving the kids who have to take it but struggled on the first exam completely screwed because there is NO curve. Exam averages are in the low to mid 60s. Almost anyone I have talked to has between a 65 and a 75 in his class. With no curve this should be illegal. Cannot imagine why anyone would want to take this guy.

He is a very nice and caring guy, but his lectures are hard to follow. He took directly from the textbook, but somehow his lectures lacked structure. I went to every lecture and consistently felt like it was a waste of my time. When I sat and listened, I gained a lot more than when I tried to write exactly what he was saying, because it was all over the place. With that being said, he is very helpful when you go to his office hours. When you take time out of your day to be there, he respects you and truly does want his students to succeed. So if you put in effort, he will give it right back. The MATLAB assignments were super easy, especially if you worked in a group- I just recommend doing those way ahead of time so you aren't waiting until the last minute. I used Chat on all of them, and for the most part, it was accurate, still good to check it yourself, though, because you could lose a few points here or there (like I did). My one beef with Conway is that he doesn't give you practice exams that are his, and for the ones he does give you, he doesn't provide answer keys. So going into the first exam, I felt very unprepared because I didn't know his exam style, and that reflected in my grade, however, I was able to get it up. He asks a lot more theoretical questions than you would expect, so know the concepts and know them well, not just how to solve a problem. I liked him enough as a person, though, to take him again for 241, so take that as you will. My best advice is to go to his office hours and don't take shortcuts.

Posts his lecture videos so you never really have to go to class. Discussion is optional other than showing up for quizzes. Tests and quizzes are extremely fair. Just study a little bit before and you should be fine. Take this guy for calc 3

I took this professor’s class back at a community college last spring and it was a ton of work. Pros: Very Very Very generous grading policy. 6 quizzes were dropped, lowest exam was dropped, lowest matlab was dropped, and there were at least like 20 extra credit opportunities in the class. Also in my experience the exams were very similar to the practice exams. She is very organized, she has lecture notes, study guides, practice exams, and has a schedule for you to complete them by so you are ready to succeed. More neutral stuff I have my own hatred of the proctoring of the exams, but I hated the asynchronous proctoring of the exams much more than the exams themselves. I felt exams were pretty standard and I could deal with them. I did not get to know her a lot as since it was asynchronous I never had a class with her. As many people said she goes slowly, which is amazing for a class like 246 but it would be too slow for me so I would just read the textbook. I also got lazy at the end of the class which was not the move because the final exam was a week after the third midterm. Also the matlabs were mostly fine but one of them just didn’t work for me. All in all, hard class, but the professor has great organization. I don’t know what she’s like personally, but I think she wants you to succeed.

Professor Halperin is an extremely nice guy who cares about his students. The class at first is hard to understand but over time it gets better. Every exam is from the textbook which is really nice. In class it is sometimes hard to understand what is going on. Many people skip class and you can but I recommend you go since many times he goes over hw answers.
Very fun class, the professor kept the activities fun and his teaching style was generally relaxed but still made sure to cover the topics well

Ebrahimian is a very effective teacher. The best thing about his class is that he engages students and lets students finish proofs. If you want to learn material well, take his class. However, he makes the grading a bit harder than is really necessary, and has HW due every single class.

Adams is a fantastic professor. He always comes prepared to class and does a great job helping his students through difficult problems. I would recommend him highly if you get a chance to take one of his courses.

Dr. Ramachandran is, hands down, the best college professor I've ever had. He is extremely knowledgeable, is very good at communicating information and is a very nice man who essentially embodies everything that is needed in a college professor. Let me begin by admitting that his class was very challenging. The homeworks were tough, the average on the two midterms probably averaged out at a 59 (there was a very generous curve at the end of the course) and you won't get very far by lollygagging and mindlessly memorizing a few formulas. That being said, I thoroughly learned about an immense (almost unbelievable) amount of difficult and very important mathematical concepts and I am very, very happy that I took the course with him. After having taken Rama's course I honestly consider myself a much more mature and knowledgeable mathematician than I did before I took his course (and I had straight As in math beforehand). I guess I should also warn you that Ramachandran is not for everyone. A lot of people in my class didn't like it at all and claimed that he was a bad professor for various lame reasons. Usually, their reasoning was something like, "He's all over the place and is impossible to follow," or, "I feel like we don't learn anything in the class". What that illustrates is that they're not accustomed to rigorous, difficult math courses and that they're either too lazy or not apt enough to study and understand the deeper concepts that are actually worth putting the time and effort in for. One kid in the class said that "Modular arithmetic is dumb because there are no formulas." If you associate yourself with people like that then I recommend dropping out of any upper-level math courses and taking something more your style like communications. In summation, I highly recommend Dr. Ramachandran to anyone who is a serious and mature student and/or to anyone who wants to learn some awesome math. If you're in it for the easy A then take he class with someone else. P.S. His grading is very fair; it's just that his problems and homeworks are challenging and take a fair amount of time and effort to complete.
Boring lectures. Course contents are exactly the same as the textbook. But the midterm means are not bad.
The best professor. Smiles always and tells funny stories about his children. Exam grades sometimes rough (uniform distribution between 0 and 100) but fair.

Beware, his homework is impossible. I would always go to the physics help classroom and spend 3 hours there with other students from this class. However his tests are not bad and he's a nice guy so if you know what he lectures on you will do fine on the tests.

First off, I hope you don't have Ninad as a TA. Second, the professor was very dry and I couldn't tell if he actually cared about teaching. Everyone said the lectures are useles so I stopped coming to class. The key to get at least a B is to do good on the homework and lab reports. Tophat is used the entire course and the curve is amazing. I heavily bombed every exam (including the final) and still got out with a B. Also, didn't learn a single thing.

this is the WORST CLASS IVE EVER TAKEN at UMD but SHE IS AMAZING. Dr. H is very kind, and explains things so well in lecture. Her exams are incredibly fair, some of the problems are exactly the same as in lecture or her practice midterms. She did not curve since the averages were pretty high but she did curve the final by 10 points out of 120 so about 8%. She also dropped the lowest midterm which was nice. btw the final was DIABOLICAL. the most insane exam I have ever taken, I barely got the points I needed to pass and for context my two highest midterms were a 64 and an 80 so yeah it was very bad. Quizzes were easy, TA always went over similar problems right before. But yeah if you get the chance take any class you can with her!!!! She's amazing

Physics is a really boring class at times. Milchberg is never boring. His only flaws are that he goes into too much detail and can be a little disorganized. If you like physics or math or are majoring in one of those you will love his class. He really knows his stuff and he is very nice and is also fair and listens to his students. He asks questions to the class and if you have a questions he will really try to get you an answer, he wants you to succeed and learn. If you are an engineering major you may struggle a bit. His lectures will bog you down with fine details and things that you may not have to care about or may not apply to you. His lectures are also almost entirely conceptual which can be hard for engineers who are used to building things and using numbers physical literal examples. His grading scale is very generous, the homeworks are textbook problems that you have 2 weeks to do and while his exams are hard, he will only count your higher midterms and if you do better than either midterm on the final he will use your final exam grade as 80% of your total grade. This class isn't a lot of work and honestly if you show up and take notes and pay attention you will be fine.

I am three weeks into this class so take it with a grain of salt. I am tired of him treating class like discussions. I am tired of him wasting time telling us to take our hoodies off, our headphones out, etc. He will use the entire class time to talk about how he teaches and does not teach us the material. He leaves us with a PDF to self-learn. This isn't a good way to expend tuition money.

Ok this is specifically in response to all the genuinely spiteful reviews on here. I'm not here to judge who is and who isn't a liar or who is and who isn't incompetent. But it looks like this entire struggle's been brought on by the lack of communication between the Professor and the students. As someone who had Prof Jahedi the semester before last, I can confirm she's very easy to approach and talk with. That would help a lot with having the information you need to understand why the course is structured a certain way. Bashing the Professor like some of the reviews do below is a bit reprehensible when she's a human being. Think this entire thing is a miscommunication issue that can be avoided.
Weekly quizzes to boost your grade, homeworks are easy, practice exams are identical to the exams, don't know what more you need to get a free a+
Exam is impossible. I don't know what she expects of students. I came in with a full understanding of the material and the exam was impossible.

He is very smart however He does not know how to teach undergraduate classes. He write on the board all these formula and proofs that most of the class no one understands. He usually tells you about what is on the midterm however it is very difficult to review the midterm since a lot of materials are not in the book. The final project is very easy but you need to find a interesting topic. He allows you to hand in late home works. Overall his class is not difficult to get a B in because he is very generous about grading and if you get an A in his final, he gives you an A in the class.

He's an ok lecturer. I thought I understood the concepts raised in class, but no matter how much I studied and jotted down every single thing he mentioned, and went to every single class, I could not get higher than an 80 on his exams. His slides were basically all pictures, and he didn't record lectures, so you had to go to class to understand. His tests are purposely designed to trick you and, most of the time, make no sense, no matter how much you know the topic. The worksheets weren't bad, but as someone who got an A in BSCI170 and even harder science classes like anatomy, I could not do good on his exams for the life of me.

He is a nice person overall; however, for this class, he goes very fast over the slides, making it hard to understand the concepts. He tells you something won't be on the exam, but then puts it on the exam. He does not curve, but he does drop the lowest midterm grade, which is nice. The only way I got through was by going to the GSS and asking chat to explain the concepts to me. One time, I asked him to explain a question to me, and he told me it was in the slideshow and told me to study harder.

The lab itself is not difficult at all. You complete a weekly pre-lab quiz before you go to the lab, then you answer some in-lab questions during class. Sometimes there are post-lab assignments but everything is fairly easy. Usually you'll finish the lab early and you can leave. Mohan did not teach my class and we were instead taught by a TA. The TA I had was very unprofessional and unhelpful. He barely teaches and gives little to no instructions (none that made sense at least) for any of the labs or assignments even if you directly ask him questions. However, the grading is not strict so you can expect to get an A in this expect.

Dr.Lombardi is great! She's organized and very upbeat even at 9am which makes me want to learn. She also made us do a couple interactive activities in class which is SO helpful in understanding the overall concepts. Exams are fair for the most part, sometimes her short answer questions are a little too hard but besides that fair.

As a freshman, I was pretty nervous about being in STEM classes at UMD since I've heard some profs who do research are a lot less dedicated to teaching. However, Dr. Karen is definitely the best bio prof I could have taken. She is genuinely so kind and truly has a passion for teaching students biology. Her lectures are very organized, and the way she teaches is easy to understand. Her office hours are also really approachable so I felt encouraged to go to them and ask questions. As for work, there's around 11 hwks and GAE which are all graded based on completion. There are 3 midterms and a final, and your lowest midterm grade gets dropped. The exams themselves are difficult but fair. As long as you study and make a comprehensive "cheat-sheet" (she allows a single/double page cheat sheet each exam), you'll be fine. To summarize, DEFINITELY TAKE HER IF U CAN!!!

I am not sure as to why the reviews are so high. While I agree with others that this class is hard, it is made extremely more complex than needed. His lectures are always jam-packed with material containing like a paragraph of information on more than 3/4 of the slides whereas everything else is just pictures of books and animals. This doesn’t help in his exams either as the exams are so detailed specific that literally ANYTHING this professor says could be on the exam. The exams ended up being overly complex even if you do understand the concepts since everything was so “nitty-gritty”. And while I do agree he is blunt, if you can’t handle being the subject of his jokes, I would suggest moving to the back of the class. If you want a good grade I HIGHLY recommend taking another professor. The only thing that prevented I believe the majority of students from dropping out was the “lab” grade which cushioned everyone by A LOT.

Dr. Tran is very nice and understanding. She is very approachable and helpful when it comes to answering questions and receiving feedback on assignments or exam questions. Her class was a flipped classroom, which I found to be more work, as you were expected to watch her topic videos before class and actual lecture was just used as a review. I didn't like how we were never given study guides for exams. Additionally, Dr. Tran never indicated what the correct answer to clicker questions was, so if you didn't write it down in class, you'd have to somehow ask her. The lab was not that bad and boosted my grade. While there were a lot of time-consuming assignments, none of them were that difficult and they ended up really helping my grade in the end. While the class is a lot of work to keep up with, Dr. Tran is pretty reasonable. As long as you keep up to date with her videos and complete the lab assignments and projects on time, you should be fine.

You will hear that he was late consistently this semester, which is true, but it is largely due to him having a hard time with a lot of weird random stuff at home. You may have heard he is not a particularly exciting professor, which is also true. If you are seeking an exciting and deeply enriching lecture, he is not the professor for you. On the other hand, he provides a consistent and predictable (in terms of curriculum) course load that makes getting an A totally doable compared to other biology classes you will take, especially if you are a good student. Definitely recommend for any premed, this is not a hard class to succeed in if you have a little patience and a pretty normal amount of studiousness. There are small issues like boring lectures and inconsistent scheduling from the professor but for the most part you get what you put in with Dr. Frauwirth. Anyone with a crazy negative opinion is straight tweaking, dawg.

Dr. Payne has been my favorite professor since I have been here (7 semesters). I took BSCI330 with him as well and I love how passionate he is, and how he really wants us to work hard in his class. He is super quirky and is a stickler for the way you phrase a question (all in good intentions, but annoying when you want to understand a concept and not get boggled down by semantics), but overall I really enjoyed his lectures and he presented the material in a very interactive way One day we all brought in flashlights and practiced doing optical illusions. Taking MATH140 with Professor Nguyen was actually a life saver. I went into the course worried I wasn't going to be prepared for the content or the pace, but Nguyen actually made it really easy to understand the content. I will agree with some earlier comments that suggested you sit closer to the front because for this year he only did lectures on the chalkboard (so if you don't show up to lectures you're kind of out-of-luck unless you have a friend), and sometimes he can be hard to hear. He really does want his students to do well. His quizzes and midterms are super approachable if you show up for lectures. In lecture, sample problems that look basically exactly like whatever quiz you have up next are given and solved. He also sends out a sample midterm that looks almost exactly like the real one about a week before (of which we had four) and solves the problems during lecture. He's pretty funny and a good lecturer, definitely passionate about what he's teaching about (sometimes he'll talk about the mathematicians who have contributed to the stuff were studying), and overall I would suggest this class. To share some of the stuff that worked for me, * After you go over the sample midterm in lecture, copy the questions and solve them multiple times throughout the week leading up to the lecture. You can write down any questions you have about the processes and go to Math Success (tutoring) for them to help you reason out the rest. (Make sure if you go to Math Success though you already have a bit of an understanding of the concepts. They're helpful for confirmation of processes but I'm not sure how great the program is for being taught concepts from the ground up). * TALK TO YOUR TA's! They're really helpful, especially for worksheets that you do in discussion which can be super difficult. But if you understand how to do these, you'll do better than fine on the midterms. * Find previous final exams for the class and use those to study for the final. Nguyen has said, and I quote, "The midterms are heaven and the final is hell", and I believe him. So try and use previous finals to study, because they probably repeat the question style. I'm not really sure how finals are going to go (we haven't taken it yet) but the class itself sets you up well to take the blow that the final might have on your grade as long as you do decently on the midterms. * Lastly, I hate to be this person, but ya gotta show up to class. Set however many alarms you need and get in that lecture hall and ATTEND DISCUSSION. Besides the fact that you will have a graded worksheet every discussion, it is also in your best interest, and in the best interest of your grade and understanding of the topic to show up. So just go to class man.

This class is so easy to pass. She drops your two lowest grades from each section of the class- in-class assignments (which you have 3 chances total to get a 10 out of 10), homework assignments (which you have unlimited tries to get perfect score on), and R coding assignments (which are difficult in the beginning but she puts out a tutorial showing exactly what you need to code and you go over the coding in discussion). Her midterms and final are the same exact structure and order every year and she posts all the old tests, so if you just practice some of the old exams the tests will be super easy. You also don't have to memorize any equations- she gives you a sheet of all the equations you need and when you need to use each one on the tests so basically the whole test is just plugging in numbers and basic algebra (multiplication, addition, etc). A few things to note: she does have a thick accent but you get used to it and the lectures aren't recorded, but all the slides and information is posted so you don't even have to go to class if you don't want to but I recommend going because you have a lot of extra credit opportunities from being in class, she goes over a lot of examples, and you need to attend if it's an in-class activity day. Super interesting professor and class. Rewatch lectures and take notes carefully, do every practice exam, and you will be fine, also participate in the discussion. Getting an A in this class is very feasible with effort

I personally think this is a great class and I like how Dr. Tran teaches. She's also super nice, welcoming, and relatable. If you're not a fan of a flipped classroom model then here's your fair warning (I like it). The lectures are more like clicker based "discussions" to practice the concepts in the pre-lecture videos and they are broken up into bursts (5-25 mins) so honestly if you watch a video while eating a meal or like little breaks here and there you don't even need to take notes like that (because going to class is basically studying imo) Dr. Tran explains things pretty simply in the videos and in class and if you don't understand something she's pretty accessible, we picked two office hours as a class and if you still can't make it just email or ask your TA. This class has ALOT of assignments though so be prepared, it's not hard it's just tedious especially the lab presentations. Sometimes the lecture exams and the major lab assignments were kind of stacked back to back but we kind of asked (feedback through survey) to have them spaced out a bit more and Dr. Tran listened and for that second exam, lab assignment combo we were given more time (just communicate). Labs were pretty fun; there are two 2hr time slots but my section rarely ever stayed the entire 2 hours. The exams weren't particularly hard, sometimes the questions were worded oddly and I had to ask my TA for clarification a couple of times. But because of the sheer amount of assignments and points (clicker pts graded on participation, lab participation, bonus points, weekly concept check assignments "PAKs" that are graded on completion) your exam score shouldn't really tank your grade all that much. In conclusion: content is pretty easy, courseload/work is heavy, exams are medium difficulty (clarity), but bc there's so much work it truly is hard to not pass and getting an A is definitely doable.

Literally the nicest professor I have ever had. The class itself is totally doable. The exams are fair, and he usually will emphasize the topics he wants to ask about on the exams so pay attention. He records all lectures so you can rewatch to study for exams. The lab is a super grade boost and there are is a ton of built in extra credit. Take his class!

I have loved many biology professors and it pains me to dislike this one. He is a nice person but an AWFUL professor. He is terrible at explaining concepts and highly unprofessional. I sadly learned nothing from this man and wasted 3 credits. I was actually surprised when I saw how high his ratings were because I completely disagreed. Take someone else.. you will learn nothing. Class consisted of two tests and a final.

Dr. Wu is a great teacher! She truly cares about student learning, and personally hosts office hours every week where students have the opportunity to work through the homework assignments with each other and with her. She didn't test on anything she didn't cover in class, but she does cover a lot in class (and will test on things that she says but aren't written on the slides), so be sure to take thorough notes. The content is dense, but Dr. Wu wants her students to succeed and tries her best to make that happen. The class is dense in content even compared to other upper-level biology classes, but Dr. Wu will work with you to help you succeed if you put in the effort!

In my opinion Friedman is kinda funny. But! this class genuinely sucked the life out of me. The homework's took me 2-3 hours but that might have been a me problem. He doesn't record lectures, only posts notes but they can be hard to understand without context. He shifts the grading scale so a 60 is lowkey passing and a high 70 or low B is probably about an A. I will say though even with that, the average of the last midterm was a 47 and I got a 45. Overall I got a 33 on the first, a 59 on the second and a 45 on the last one. There were a lot of things he never fully went over in class though. For example I'm not sure if he ever actually explained what the general charges of elements were on a periodic table which is pretty basic and foundational stuff. If you expect him to actually teach, don't get your hopes up. He's very good when it comes to introducing a topic and then sometimes he'll do a couple examples but if you actually want to understand you gotta teach yourself. If you're good at that kind of thing and you did good in AP chem in high school you should be fine. Obviously I'm not good at teaching myself and I never took AP chem. The GSS people were really nice though. Half star for the jokes, another for the GSS. But I'm definitely failing this class. Please don't take this class if haven't taken any kind of AP chem class before. Even if you have no other choice don't do it. Save yourself. Run and never look back. :(

So this isn't really about Guest herself, because you barely see her if at all, but the course itself since she's the only instructor. The TAs basically run the whole class, and I am very lucky to have gotten a good TA. There are prelab quizzes, and they aren't that bad, however, there are refection quizzes that occur 1-2 weeks after a lab has taken place that are such a pain. They are in place of a final exam, and I do think I prefer those to a final, however, they are quite challenging and only have 2-3 questions and are around 10 points, so if you get something wrong on one of these quizzes with 3 questions, that's immediately a 66%, and like I mentioned before, they are quote challenging. The lab itself isn't horrible, but the instructions in the lab manual which Dr. Guest wrote are quite confusing, and I had to ask my TA lots of questions for the procedures to make sense. The post-lab questions for your lab reports are straightforward and pretty easy. On the lab reports, you can also get extra credit. However, this past semester, some people got over 100% in the class due to the extra credit, so basically the class had a negative curve, as I have a 94.7% in the class and that's an A-, which I am not happy about. I know some people have it worse, but as I worked very hard in that class, getting an A- with a grade that would be an A in any other circumstance really angers me, since it isn't a 4.0. This class is also only 1 credit, so it shouldn't screw my GPA as someone who is also a STEM major, but I am annoyed by it. The class takes up a lot of time with the prelab quizzes and lab reports for a 1 credit class, and as someone who took this their first semester as a freshman, it really added to the stress levels. I would recommend taking this after you have already adjusted to the workload of college, and really, this class can be a hit or miss.

Chem in general is extremely hard, for me at least, not to mention it's a weed out course. He is not helpful in lectures, once you get the first 10 clicker questions for the grade, people stopped coming to lecture since he post the lecture slides anyway. Would have attended all lectures regardless, but his lectures were honestly so boring and monotone and you're gonna have to teach yourself the content anyway since he pretty much just reads off the slides. I will say though, the practice exams were a good resource and pretty similar to the midterms. The class is already curved, so he won't curve the exams (unless its like a 30% average tho, def not if the average is like ~60%). Discussions are optional too and the slides are posted in ELMS

I already wrote a review for her but I realized I left out a very important con of taking her: her notes are actually awful. She basically just scribbles down random structures and then uploads them on canvas so if you miss class you're screwed. She also has really bad handwriting that I have trouble reading even though I have bad handwriting.

I took 232 Orgo 1 lab in Spring '24, which was honestly better than expected, definitely better than Gen Chem 1 lab. Like the other reviews, this one is more for the course itself than for Dr. Koppel. Overall, MOST of the labs weren't time-consuming and sometimes fun but the post-lab questions offered nothing but annoyance because they often had little to do with what we did in labs. I STRONGLY recommend going to office hours EVERY week, whether for the worksheets or post-lab questions. Either way, this strategy relieves unnecessary stress and guarantees a decent score on the questions. If your TA is great (like mine was), optimize their time sections. You need to maximize your points on ALL the lab reports as much as you can because THERE IS NO CURVE. Since Dr. Koppel removed midterms and finals, she no longer fancied one. Now there is only a practical "quiz" at the end of the semester, which is generally easy if you study well, BUT it can plummet your grade too since there are only two questions worth 25 points each, so don't take it lightly! Overall, complete all your assignments, study well for the practical, and most importantly go to office hours.

Organic Chemistry is a challenging class and this class can be very difficult. However, you will do well if you read the textbook and put in your efforts. Dr. Isaac’s is very knowledgeable and he’s a very kind and passionate professor. His midterms are hard but definitely doable. The final was very fair! I think this class is a reflection of the amount of hard work you put in. I would highly recommend you take Dr. Isaac’s and as long as you study a little each day, you will be fine!

Kahn is a very interesting guy. It's clear that he's incredibly knowledgeable in the field of biophysical chemistry, but it doesn't translate well into his teaching ability. He definitely loves the content and teaches as such, but it sometimes feels like he expects us to know more than we actually do, just because he's an expert at it. He sometimes spends time inefficiently in class, talking about housekeeping matters that don't pertain to the content, or bringing up MATLAB. Kahn loves MATLAB like his own child and he often depicts reactions as MATLAB graphs but he isn't the best at explaining what happens in the graph. He often left me more confused about certain concepts after he brought up the MATLAB graphs. However, one-on-one, he is very good at explaining concepts concisely if you don't understand them- i.e. go to his office hours and pre-exam review sessions and ask questions if you can, they were pretty helpful to me. All lectures and review sessions were recorded but he writes important equations and reactions on the chalkboard a lot, which isn't visible with the camera, so being present for the lectures is your best shot. He also got upset about halfway through the semester because of attendance and threatened to stop recording if attendance didn't improve. He often says that his exams are meant to be difficult, and they are, but he gives out a lot of partial credit and grades leniently. Kahn prides himself on teaching conceptual concepts over plug and chugging formulas, which is something that works well enough for me, but I had to put in a lot of time to this class to not fail. He also draws on a couple of concepts from biochem and physics. He posts all of his previous exams and a dated syllabus on his group website under biochem.umd.edu, would highly recommend checking those out. Shoutout to the discussion TA Ryan, he's the goat.
garbage. pretends to care, but does not help, even when students actually reach out. does not show up to own office hours.

As a person, he is nice. However, as a professor, I have to be plain and unbiased: he is not good! If you are reading this and have the chance to prepare, please do so in advance as soon as possible. His quizzes are difficult, but the exams are even worse than the quizzes. If you can't change your professor, make sure to prepare well in advance. But if you have the option, I strongly recommend avoiding him, or you will regret it later.

The previous reviews are pretty accurate. Pedram isn't the most interesting professor and his voice can lull you to sleep. However, the main problem I have with him are his exams. His averages were WAYY lower than those of Elias and Nora. The previous exams he provided were far easier than the exams he actually gave us this semester. On Exam 1, the only code-writing on the practice exams was doing basic things with class definition. But on the actual midterm were really strange algorithms that were difficult to understand. He doesn't really do a good job of preparing you for his midterms. His projects were also extremely boring, as every single one of them was remaking a data structure from scratch rather than using it in a cool way. Everyone took Pedram in Spring 2025 because Elias was full and Nora had really bad reviews, so everyone saw him as the 2nd best. Just do yourself a favor and take one of the other professors unless you want your grade to suffer.

He's clearly a very knowledgeable professor. Additionally, he's an approachable and is more than happy to clarify concepts that you need clarification for. So overall, as a person and instructor he's great. The only gripe are how he gives assessments. He does not prepare you at all for exams, and he will sometimes add questions relating to one very esoteric or specific thing that he talked about once during lecture and not present in any lecture slides, lab assignments, and projects. Additionally, he'll sometimes give past exams or worksheets, but these also do not reflect the type of questions in exams. So, this is what makes his exams a lot more challenging. You will do fine in the class as long as you're not doing unrelated stuff on your laptop or phone like playing brawl stars or doom scrolling. Pay attention during lecture, take and REVIEW notes, and you will be fine. I believe he gives a reasonable curve at the end, I think a 75 is a B.

I really enjoyed having Fawzi as a proffessor. His lectures were engaging and I never really felt bored while in them. He can be a little cringe from time to time but honestly, that adds to the atmosphere. People get on him for being overly picky with grading, and while I also have encountered this, if you pay attention and go to lecture he gives you all the tools you need to succeed. The biggest issue for me was the no recording lectures thing so you really have to be there. I think I could have easily gotten an A if I had shown up at every lecture. He also has pop quizzes in discussion so you want to be in a later discussion and make friends in the earlier ones.

Max is goated idc what the other reviews say. He's probably the most engaging CS lecturer I've had at UMD. He doesn't bog you down with basically any math, you just need to know the general concepts and how to apply them in a real project. He's still very disorganized, and his exams are obviously very polarizing, but I feel like I actually learned a lot from this class. Despite his slides being in a constant state of chaos, he's very good at explaining difficult concepts and tying them to interesting real world examples. His AI ethics lecture in particular was genuinely fantastic. All the HWs are super easy to get full credit on, and imo his exams are not bad at all. If you listen to him in lecture and retain his main points, then an hours worth of study before the exam is all you need. To be clear, for any class other than CMSC320, take somebody else. I cannot imagine having him for a class as rigorous as 250 or 351. But if you want to learn how to do data science and machine learning in the real world, take Max.

He is a kind person that really cares about how you're doing. You gotta be quick with your fingers if you wanna be able to answer all the clicker questions. The amount of times I missed a clicker was so many :(

The GOAT. Hilarious class. Exams are half running through and analyzing algorithms, half creating your own new algorithms based on existing ones and analyzing them (the hard part). Super lenient on dates, and listens to the class. Lectures are flipped and therefore basically optional, but you'll want to go to them for some of the more important topics and after exams. Your 3 'quizzes' a week are straight from recorded lectures so a small portion of your grade is just free. If you're 1 standard deviation ahead on exams, you get curved to an A. Which shouldn't be too hard with all these salty plebs giving 1 stars. Congratulations.

Pros: - All exams were timed, open note, and open internet. They were not structured to be extra difficult because of this caveat. The final was supposed to be in person, but got moved online. - The goals for assignments (home works and projects) were fairly clear. It takes some time to adapt to Marsh's "unique" approach to projects in the class, but office hours and campuswire were always open and the instructors actually answered questions (Most of my previous class piazzas had questions ignored on piazza) - Marsh genuinely cares about the course. Cons: - Lectures are asynchronous. You watch the lectures in your own time, and the lecture itself was a "discussion". I attended almost every in person lecture, and it was a waste of time. - All of his projects are graded with bash and python scripts, and you submit through a gitlab commit. You will always have that feeling in the back of your head that the project might not run the same on his system. - This class has A TON of overhead knowledge. C, docker, git, bash, python, linux, etc. You aren't expected to be an expert, but you will spend a lot of time learning content independent of the class just so you can do the projects. Overall I recommend 414 with Marsh. This is the CS class I had the best experience in. It doesn't hold your hand, but help is there if you need it. It is structured in a way where you ACTUALLY LEARN stuff on your own. With that in mind, you have to put in work to do well in this class. Do not expect this class to be a free A unless you already have security knowledge.

Marsh for 417 was great. He took a systems approach to the whole class which I really liked. If you didn't like 216 then you'll have a rough time, but projects are easy as long as you can read manpages and use Wireshark. It's impossible to fail his class if you submit even a half-assed attempt on all the projects. All exams including the final were take-home. If you don't get an A in the class it's on you

His class reminds me of CMSC351 with Kruskal. A lot of the content is pretty analytical and some of the homeworks can be tough, but overall he grades very leniently and gives lot of partial credit. Projects are pretty fair and if people ask they will extend the deadlines a bit usually. Overall, I think its a pretty rewarding class.

I made a review back in November regarding Prof Tokekar and I would say that his management of the 421 course improved between then and the end of the semester. Pros: 1) Posts lecture slides and links to additional online resources and textbook chapters to review 2) Mix of online and in-person OH and TAs did a good job at answering questions during OH 3) Interesting assignments and projects 4) Answers questions during lecture, OH, and is very flexible 5) Posts practice exams and problems to prepare for final and midterm 6) Allows regrade requests 7) Quickly graded final exams Cons: 1) Took a while for midterms to be graded and transferred to ELMS 2) TAs took a little while to respond to Piazza posts

Let’s start with the pros. The course teaches you a decent amount of concepts about different database systems, how to design them, and how to work with each. The projects were a lot of fun and taught me most of what I know about databases. I would say you could finish a project in a day or two if you understand the concepts. With all that being said.. the homeworks and exams are MISERABLE. Amol has HUNDREDS of slides on a subject, but they don’t really teach you much. He does go in depth about some subjects in class, but a lot of it is left to self teaching (go figure, it’s a CS course). I wouldn’t take this course again. A lot of what I found to be useful can be learned on your own if you follow some advanced SQL book and lookup Apache spark and mongodb. The last 4 weeks of class are mostly useless, as he goes into how database programs are implemented. It may seem useful at first, but there are just so many concepts to memorize. I’m giving the class 3 stars because I enjoyed the projects. The other material was insane. On the bright side, there is a pretty generous curve.

I do not even know where to start with this class. The lectures were just the professor rambling about some random bullshit. He would draw some functions and diagrams on the board and then show some math but it was all pointless. It went to the point where out of 80 students only like 20 would come to class. I came once to class just to see wtf was happening and I found half the kids watching the world cup match. You were pretty much left in the dark, the concepts from class did not help at all and your only salvation was to hope there was something online to help you. The TA's did not even look at the code, this was pretty evident because for some reason the class avg on these projects was a 90-95%. They primarily graded based off of the reports. To add to the glory of this weird class, for the fourth project the TA's never updated installation instructions and after a week of complaints they just decided to give everyone a 100% and anyone who managed to get something working extra credit. And thus every group got between 100-220% on this project worth 20% of the grade. I cant say I really learned anything from this class tbh. It seems cool and the topics seem cool but I really didnt learn or gain anything besides maybe losing sanity. Though i will say minimal effort is required for this 3 credit 400 level cs course

Aric’s definitely one of the best professors on campus. Coming with mediocre python skills, his class challenges your growth and understanding starting from the basics to more convoluted subjects. He’s generous with extensions and office hours. All his UTA’s are very helpful and available. Don’t slack on practices, late penalty is 50%.

horrible teacher, half of the class doesn't even come, she's rude when someone ask a question, she's thinks that we are suppose to know everything because we took previous calculus classes in high school which I indeed don't, she also just writes the answers on the chalk board or show them already written as if that is helping us when we still don't know what's going on, her accent is very strong so be aware, discussions In my opinion are pointless if I still don't understand what's going on, I don't even attend class anymore because of how bad she is as a teacher. whatever you do please don't take her and find a different professor.

I think I mainly disliked this class because the content is pretty difficult and if you're someone that doesn't like math or isn't great with it then you may have a hard time. Dr. Ebrahimian does do a pretty good job at lecturing and doesn't give any homework. He's a funny guy and his TAs are all really good. Conway is overall a great professor! I didn't go to his lectures because it seemed pointless to me, especially when his lecture notes were dense and provided online (even the recordings too, though the quality isn't that good). I personally found his quizzes to be a bit challenging to me, but looking back at it, I realized they were actually darn easy, it's just that I was having a rough semester. Exams, unlike what others have said in the reviews, are actually pretty do able and easy (I always end up doing much better on the exams than on the quizzes). Yes he does test you on the nitty gritty concepts, but I actually kinda liked that because Conway will do an amazing job teaching you linear on a deeper level, and helping you get a deeper intuition behind it (and it's just like 1 or 2 questions at most that are like nitty gritty, most are just general linear exam questions to expect). You will definitely want this kind of professor if linear is like a core/key foundation behind your major (a la computer science). You also don't get any weekly homework assignments but rather 4 major MATLAB assignments that you can work with a group. They aren't that bad and it's kinda do able too. He is very nice and approachable, and funny too. Definitely take 240 with him it's worth it.

Professor Conway is a great Calc 3 professor. He lectures very well and provides ample resources to complete the course. His exams are always fair. The questions are always iterations of text book problems and the directions are always clear. Professor Conway does not assign graded homework, rather he posts suggested text book problems. There is a quiz every week in the course that relates to the material covered in lecture and the suggested practice problems. Professor Conway is a kind professor and happy to answer questions and happy to be teaching the course. Would recommend

If you take this professor: - The MATLAB assignments are horrible. You are simply assigned problems and expected to figure them out yourself. Now, this wouldn't be too bad if the textbook were alright. But that isn't the case. In particular, the textbook you must use is so out of date that many of the features they teach you literally don't work in MATLAB anymore, and you're going to need to spend significant time searching the web and/or attending tutoring to get help on solving the problems. Make sure to start the MATLAB assignments early. On the bright side, based on grading statistics, almost everyone got a full score on all their MATLABS, so as long as you at least mostly solve all the problems, you should be fine. - There is no point attending his lectures, as he is the worst lecturer I have ever seen. He talks in a very soft, monotone voice, and rambles without an organized train of thought. It's hard to follow what he's saying, and many people (including me) got up and left in the middle of the first lecture. Your time is significantly better spent self-studying for this class. - Make sure to attend all discussions. The people who had Chirag as their TA seem to have raving reviews about him, but as someone who didn't have him as my TA, I can attest that the quality of discussions can vary wildly depending on who your TA is. On top of this, there usually isn't enough time to solve all discussion problems in the discussion section. For both these reasons, make sure to individually work through all discussion problem sets yourself. - Grillakis posts notes from David Levermore, but Levermore's notes are borderline unintelligible and unreadable, even if you are experienced in reading math-heavy papers. In my opinion, Levermore's ability to explain a topic, no matter how simple, is almost as bad as Grillakis's ability to lecture on a topic. Levermore's notes are good for one thing, and one thing only: they have a lot of practice problems, usually with decent explanations of the solutions. Many people will tell you that Justin Wyss-Gallifent's diffeq notes are very useful for self-studying. Aside from the occasional typo (and the rare provably untrue statement), this is true, but what they don't tell you is that HIS NOTES DO NOT COVER THE ENTIRE LAST 1/3 OF THE CURRICULUM. Neither do Grillakis's lecture slides, and, if I'm remembering correctly, neither do Levermore's notes (barring some exceptions, in particular Green's functions). This course provides you with (almost) no materials for all topics between the second midterm and the common final, and this nearly caused me a mental breakdown in the days leading up to the final. Which brings me to my most important point: - Get to know someone who has a different diffeq professor, and have them send you all of their resources and practice exams. If this isn't possible, at least go to the Guided Study Session for diffeq in the days leading up to the final and download all the materials they give you there. I personally learned the entire last 1/3 of the curriculum from a single practice exam with solutions that my friend (who had Francisco Arana Herrera) sent me, two days before the final. I had long been of the opinion that it doesn't matter what professor you take a class with, as you can always self-study your way to a good grade. Taking diffeq with Grillakis single-handedly convinced me otherwise. Although it is true that you can always self-study your way to a good grade, having a bad professor can add an unnecessary amount of stress, work, and overall mental burden, ESPECIALLY if you aren't even provided with the proper materials to study the topics yourself. But with that aside, if you work hard enough, it is indeed possible to succeed in this class. I personally got a full 100 on both midterms (for which the upper quartiles were 90 and 84 respectively), and I even ended up outscoring my friend on the final (albeit only because he made a careless mistake). But even with all the curves (all I know is my 96.7 became an A+) and relatively easy (depending on who you ask) midterms, if I could do it over again, I would without hesitation take a different professor, or even better yet, take diffeq from a community college.
Homework is the same problems as the exams, IDENTICAL. He even offers extra credit on each exam by dropping a question and making it extra credit.
This guy is the goat. Every midterm is take home, and he goes over the questions with different numbers in class right before releasing the midterm.

Since I withdrew from the course about halfway through the semester, I normally would not review the professor except I don't want other math majors to make the same mistake I did. For the record, this is the first course I ever dropped with a W. HOWEVER, he is not a good professor unless you are already naturally brilliant at math. Macasieb is great. She understands number theory in and out, and communicates it very well to her students. Lectures are focused on going through basic proofs of the material, and a sufficient number of examples for you to understand what's going on. If you skip class, you can just read the book; it's essentially the same thing. Grades consist of weekly homework from the book (lowest 1-2 grades dropped), weekly quizzes that are homework problems verbatim (again, lowest few dropped), two midterms, and a cumulative final. Exam questions are either computational (and thus simple) or proof-based (almost always come from problems in the textbook that are recommended but not explicitly assigned). Exam averages suck (we're talking 55-65ish), so she will obviously curve a bit in the end. Advice to do well: keep up with the material (early concepts such as Fermat's theorem and modulo arithmetic definitely impact the later material substantially), do extra practice problems from the book. This class requires a bit of work, but if you put in the effort, you'll be fine.

Probably the worst professor I have ever had. Completely fails to engage students during lectures. He is disorganized, constantly had to delay an exam and couldnt get through all the material by the end of the course. His first exam had typos that changed the questions and one question said, and I quote, "make sense of the function". This is in a proof based math course. His handwriting is completely illedgible which means you cannot catch up on lectures if you miss something and cannot use his notes at all. Why this man is allowed to teach the most notoriously challenging math class at UMD is beyond me.

He really cares about his students. He explains concepts extremely clearly and encourages you to think about what's going on in class. I never had to use the textbook because his notes are so clear. Tests are difficult enough to let you see if you actually are understanding the material, but not so difficult that you feel like crap after taking them. I also took the MATLAB course. The tutorial was really helpful and clear. I spent maybe 10 hours total the entire semester on this class, and that includes learning MATLAB from scratch and doing the projects. Take this class as early as possible; it's easy, not a lot of work, and a decent introduction to MATLAB.

Course: This is a course on Electromagnetism. Concepts will be harder to understand than those from Physics I because they relate to more abstract concepts, but as long as you spend a good amount of time understanding those concepts the exams shouldn't be a hard time. According to the schedule Hailu is supposed to go up to Chapter 16 in the textbook and even talk about Thermodynamics, but this semester and I think the last semester as well he only got up to Chapter 14. So just keep that in mind. Lecture: Hailu is a pretty slow lecturer and often goes through pretty long derivations and also spends quite a bit of time on practice problems. I found this approach useful to me but if you find yourself relying on the textbook a lot to understand the concepts it might not be the best idea to go to lecture. The only thing is Hailu doesn't post his lecture notes or records (unless class is canceled), and in my opinion his walkthroughs of the lecture problems are really important. So if you plan to not come to lecture try to get a friend who does go to share their notes with you. Discussion: Hailu claims you learn new material in discussion but pretty much all the discussions were just reviewing concepts from lecture. If you are good with what was in the lecture there isn't much reason to go to discussion. My TA in particular seemed to do problems that were way harder than the ones Hailu gave in lecture or in the exams. Main benefit of discussion is you can discuss HW problems with the TA. Homework: Homeworks are pretty easy for the most part as they mostly resemble lecture problems, and a lot of them just involve you deriving formulas (that were already covered in lecture) and then substituting in the values. You get 5 tries with each open-ended problem and no points are taken off until you use up all 5 tries, so use them wisely. Homeworks come every week and are due the next week. The homework is also really good practice for the exams so I'd recommend studying those problems before them. Quizzes: Quizzes are only worth 10% of the grade and there were only 8 of them this semester. One of them was also dropped. These mostly cover conceptual questions, so review the posted slides and lecture problems prior to doing these quizzes. If you get a question wrong your quiz grade can drop quite a bit, but like I said they are only 10% so don't worry too much about not doing good on these. Just make sure you aren't consistently bombing the quizzes by studying the material beforehand. Exams: Each exam consisted of 3 questions (6 for the final) with multiple parts. Hailu likes to have his questions build on each other so you'll want to make sure you understand the relationships between the concepts you learn in class and relationships built across the chapters. Hailu allows you to use an equation sheet. I'd recommend filling that sheet with every equation he covers in lecture, as the exams can consist of any question type. As long as you understand the concepts Hailu's exams aren't really too difficult, as once you figure out the concept and which equation to use the actual question becomes very simple. Other Random Advice - Don't go too crazy studying practice problems. Study the lecture problems and HW problems and if you understand those, you should be good. If you don't understand them, then you may want to try your hand at the extra textbook problems. - Use discussion/office hours to clarify concepts. - Hailu curves the class in the sense that if the class average is below what it should be, he'll make it so 20% get A's, 40% get B's, 25% get C's, the rest get D or F. So as long as you put in a decent effort you shouldn't worry too much about failing this class, even if you aren't so good with physics. Class Review: My 4-star rating is mostly because of how easy the exams are, as they made the class a lot less stressful for me. Otherwise Hailu is mostly an average professor for me. He goes over the material decently well and he goes over many problems in class. The main caveat is he doesn't post solutions or record, which felt unnecessary since I'm sure neither of those things are very hard to do and would have made reviewing the lecture problems a lot less of a hassle. Overall, if you take PHYS260 with Hailu you really shouldn't have too much of a problem. Putting in the effort should be enough to get a decent grade.

He understands how it feels to be a student and feel confused, so he is very conscientious about how he should teach thoroughly. He is very humble as well and genuinely wants the best from his students.

Like others have said, exam questions are directly from the homeworks (so you should definitely do them) but his lectures can sometimes be very confusing. He is always available in his office though to go over hw problems and concepts from class.
Actually the best professor ever, very engaging lecturer and has take home exams and no final exam. Would 1000% recommend

It is difficult to describe why Dr. Cohen is such a horrible math professor. He goes really really fast and skips tons and tons of steps to the point where he becomes incomprehensible. To make matters worse, his handwriting is awful. He is unprepared for lectures. Several times he has thrown terms into his lectures that we'd never heard of before, and then two classes later he would explain what they are. I strongly recommend not taking Cohen. Math403 has been the most challenging course I have taken as an undergraduate, and he makes it infinitely more difficult. I am graduating with Latin honors, so I am not dumb, and I have dealt with some pretty awful professors, but this guy is the absolute worst. I guarantee you will regret taking him.

She obviously knows number theory really well but her lectures were devoted more to proving theorems which really weren't tested at all. Also all of the proofs were in the book anyway so she could have just said "for details on the proof for theorem x consult the book." Also her grader was quite draconian and if you said something like "I lost 8/10 points for an arithmetic error", she would say "if you want I could maybe give you a few points back" and then spend a few minutes continuing to expand on how you were wrong which was quite annoying.

Professor Long is one of the best math professors at UMD. He's charismatic, funny, and explains content really well. All of his lectures are from the book so you know exactly what he's talking about & his homework are fair with fair grading. The only flaw he has is planning -- or really lack of planning. The second exam was made two weeks before finals & homeworks are randomly assigned (although always with 1 full week to complete). If you're okay with not being totally certain what your upcoming week is going to look like, take him for 410. Imo it's a worth while trade off for his teaching.

Grillakis is a well-dressed man who knows this class in and out. Lectures are spent proving theorems, often differently from how the book does it, which can be helpful. Grades are the average of your homework grade (lowest of 7 dropped), your midterm average (lowest of 3 dropped), and your final exam score. Homework is often either plug-n-chug application or intense proof that you may need to go to office hours for help on. However, there is at least a week and a half between due dates, so you always have enough time to complete the assignments. Exams are basically a practical application of the material you learn. He does not put dense proofs on exams, but rather he tests your basic and superficial understanding of the techniques you learn in class. Exams can be tricky, but they are very doable and very much test your understanding of the material. Just as was said in the review below, this class is essentially a multi-dimensional extension of 410. Some of the concepts are very arcane and difficult to grasp (example, proving Stokes Theorum and boundary proofs with Jordan Contents), but Grillakis is great at explaining these concepts.

Professor Shawhan is a great teacher. He doesn't do that many problems in class and the homework is difficult but in the end, that's how you learn. I really came out of this course with a solid understanding of the basic concepts, which is key to doing well on the MCAT. Take Shawhan! An A is definitely doable as long as you can follow the textbook, which is pretty good. He posts all of his notes online after class which is a really big plus.

I took him last year for 131 and 132 and honestly he's not bad. The class itself will make you cry and throw up if you care not feeling lost. However, you're good if you're fine with being lost most of the time. The material honestly just sucks bio+physics is a horrible combo. BUT you will do well in the course. Failed all the exams but did well on hw, reading and labs and did well overall. The curve is a blessing honestly. Severson is a chill dude and honestly I found him very funny. The echo in the lecture room and lighting sucks though and makes you want to sleep so I would recommend just listening to the recordings or reading the slides and self-teaching.

She sets you up for success in her class. Lectures are fast, but filled with practice problems. She posts both her lecture notes and her slides. ExpertTA homework is fair, if tedious, and 2 free attempts are provided for each question, so give them a genuine attempt. Exams were also very fair, and one midterm was dropped as well. Discussion quizzes were whatever, but one of them was dropped. The practice problems she provides prepare you well for the exams, make sure to start them early and really understand them. Make sure to check/use Piazza, she provides a lot of answers/guidance for many homework problems and practice problems. I fell asleep during lecture a lot (not because she was boring I was just severely sleep-deprived) but I still managed to get most of the content, and anything I missed I could get from content posted. I didn't go to office hours or anything, so I didn't know her personally very well, but she seems to have good vibes and care a lot about her students' success! Everyone I know who went to office hours said they were helpful. Taylor's discussions were great as well.

A breath of fresh air in the UMD physics department. His exams are well worded, direct and do a good job of fairly assessing whether or not you fully understand the material. He shows a great deal of passion towards engineering and physics concepts, which make the otherwise semi-dull content easier to pay attention to and understand. He makes good jokes, constantly asks students if they have any questions, and is overall a professor who has compassion and an understanding of his students. This course isn't necessarily easy, but with Baden it has been a much smoother ride than in my past Physics courses. My one slight on him is that he rarely, if ever, updates canvas, but he hands back exam grades in class so you will always have a rough estimate of your grade at all times. Overall great guy, great professor and great for his students sanity.

She's a very nice woman but in lecture I never really understood what she was saying, and her voice just got a little annoying after a while. After the first exam I pretty much stopped going to lecture and only studied the previous exams she posts since the exams never change.
